children.value: With gaze and cursor on one clock (
Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Synchronization

), this chapter compares where participants look with where they move: how far the gaze runs ahead of the hand, whether gaze and cursor visit the other latent state before the first net, how the gaze and the cursor at the end of the anticipation phase relate to the first net, and how the spread of the gaze compares with the spread of the cursor. Each measure is related to the instruction condition, the questionnaire scores and the general questionnaire factor.

, the mouse-tracking trials (curvature and direction changes of token 1), the fixation-based gaze entropy of the eye-tracking analysis, the questionnaire scores and the general questionnaire factor, and the strategy rates after events. Output:
87 participants (None 32, Partial 35, Full Instructions 20), 15,177 usable trials; 86 with questionnaire scores, 77 with a general-factor score. Measures are defined in the synchronization chapter.

: GEE across trials clustered by participant (binomial for 0/1 measures, Gaussian otherwise); contrasts Full vs None + Partial (c3) and Partial vs None (c21); score slope per SD across conditions (y ~ score + c3 + c21), and slopes within each condition and their pairwise differences (y ~ score × (c3 + c21)). Benjamini–Hochberg q values across the measures of one score, measure set (eye–hand, competition, anticipation, entropy) and trial set, are in the CSV files; the text gives estimates and p, with the general factor as the main score. From placement onset, the gaze reaches the location of token 1 after a median of 508 ms and the cursor after 590 ms; the gaze arrives first in 66 % of the trials with both arrivals. Median lead 95 ms; participant means 134 ms (None 147, Partial 117, Full 144 ms). The press follows the gaze arrival by a median of 643 ms.
(movement of more than one slot): median lead 75 ms, gaze first in 64 %; participant means 162 / 185 / 205 ms (None / Partial / Full).
the gaze is at the pressed slot in 87 % of the token-1 presses and 83 % of the later presses (median distance 0.8–1.0°), and already at the next token’s location in 7–9 %.
No differences in lead, gaze at the click, gaze ahead, gaze–cursor distance or lag (all p ≥ .09).

With higher STICSA trait scores the lag at which gaze and cursor agree best is shifted toward the gaze leading (general factor +16 ms per SD, p = .030; STICSA trait +23 ms, p < .001). The token-1 lead is longer with higher general-factor scores (+20 ms per SD, p = .019), and within Full Instructions with higher STICSA trait (+39 ms, p = .002), STICSA state (+33 ms, p = .006) and general-factor scores (+33 ms, p = .006).

During the first movement the gaze is about 6–7° from the cursor (it is already at the target while the cursor leaves the centre) and the distance closes to 1.5–2° at the press. The mean distance is not associated with the condition or any score (all p ≥ .38). In None, participants with high STICSA trait show a larger distance at the end of the movement on average, with a wide spread across participants.

(participant means, stable trials): the gaze visits the other state on 4.0 % of these trials, the cursor on 7.6 %. Classes: both 1.5 %, gaze only (covert) 2.5 %, cursor only 6.1 %, neither 90 %. About half of the gaze visits (51 %) begin before the cursor starts to move.
When the gaze visits the other state, the cursor does so as well on 37 % of the trials, against 3–9 % otherwise (+2.24 log-odds, odds ratio 9.4, p < .001;

), and the deviation of the first movement toward the other state is larger (log(1 + maximum deviation) +0.59, p < .001). On the same trials, more fixation time at the other state in the prediction window goes with more pull (+0.041 per SD, p = .003, stable trials), and a first fixation at the other state goes with token 1 at the other state (+1.16 log-odds, p < .001;

On 18 % of these trials the other state receives a later net in the same trial. Gaze at the other state before token 1 makes a later net there more likely (+0.36 log-odds, p = .033, with the cursor visit in the same model), the cursor visit does not (−0.11, p = .40). Gaze at the other state in the anticipation phase predicts a later net there more strongly (+0.61, p < .001). Between participants, the rate of later splits goes with the split strategies after events (split at t+1 ρ = .67, at t+2 after transitions ρ = .64, transitions followed at t+1 ρ = −.55;
); the rate of covert visits is not related to any strategy (|ρ| ≤ .18).

Cursor-only visits are more frequent with instructions (Partial vs None +0.68 log-odds, p = .014; Full vs None + Partial +0.53, p = .014), as is the pull (Partial vs None +0.13, p = .006; Full +0.12, p = .030). Gaze visits to the other state do not differ between conditions (p ≥ .19).
Across conditions none of the visit measures is associated with a score (all p ≥ .095). Within conditions:

higher STICSA trait and BDI-II scores go with more cursor-only visits (+0.28 and +0.24 log-odds per SD, p = .007) and more pull (STICSA trait +0.068, p < .001; BDI-II +0.048, p = .005); gaze visits are not associated (p ≥ .05).

higher STICSA trait and BDI-II scores go with fewer cursor visits (−0.33, p = .003; −0.46, p < .001); higher STICSA state scores go with more gaze visits (+0.22, p = .022) and more covert visits (+0.27, p = .013); higher OCI scores with more later splits (+1.46, p < .001).

At the end of the anticipation phase the cursor lies near the centre on 41 % of the trials, the last fixation on 25 %. When away from the centre, the last fixation is at the location of token 1 on 65 % of the trials, the cursor on 39 %; gaze and cursor are at the same location on 37 %. The gaze predicts the first net better with Full Instructions (+0.36 log-odds, p = .043) and with higher OCI scores (+0.12 per SD, p = .042; within Full: IUS +0.38, p = .007); the cursor location and the agreement of gaze and cursor are not associated with the condition or the scores (p ≥ .15).

Gaze entropy, task locations (fixations, anticipation; bits)

Across conditions, only the fixation-based gaze entropy in the anticipation phase is associated with the scores (STICSA state −0.063 bits, p = .009; STICSA trait −0.057, p = .025; OCI −0.053, p = .021), and this goes together with fewer fixations (
). The gaze sector entropy and the cursor entropy are not associated with any score in either phase (all p ≥ .064).

The first movements of participants with higher STICSA trait in None look more spread out because they curve more and change direction more often, and deviate more toward the other state; the spatial entropy of the cursor, i.e. how the cursor’s time is spread over the circle, is not higher.

Gaze and cursor do not show opposite entropy effects: within None, neither gaze nor cursor entropy is associated with STICSA trait. The lower gaze entropy with higher scores across conditions comes mainly from Partial Instructions and from fewer fixations.

In None, the movement shows more competition with higher STICSA trait (curvature, direction changes, pull, cursor-only visits to the other state), while the gaze does not visit the other state more often.

Questionnaire effects within and between conditions
Gaze and cursor are aligned to about ±1.5 ms at placement onset after correcting a clock drift of 60 ppm.

The gaze reaches the location of the next net before the cursor (participant means 134 ms for token 1 and 181 ms for later tokens; medians across trials 95 and 75 ms) and stays there until the click; with higher STICSA trait and general-factor scores the gaze runs further ahead.

Gaze and cursor visits to the other state before the first net are rare (4 % and 8 %) and strongly coupled; covert visits (gaze only) are as rare as visits by both. Gaze at the other state predicts a later net there, the cursor visit does not. Instructions increase cursor visits, not gaze visits. In None, higher STICSA trait and BDI-II go with cursor visits and pull, not with gaze visits.
The last fixation before placement predicts the location of the first net better than the cursor does.

Gaze and cursor entropy agree during placement and are unrelated in the anticipation phase. The anxiety-related spread of the first movement in None is curvature and direction changes, not entropy, and it has no counterpart in gaze entropy.
